n: This lecture covers the examination of sexual conditions. In the investigation of various criminal cases and the hearing of civil cases, a need arises for forensic medical examination of sexual conditions. This examination is ordered to establish sex, sexual maturity, virginity, reproductive capacity, pregnancy, and previous delivery or abortion.

The need to establish true sex arises in several situations. First, when sex was incorrectly determined at birth. Second, when issuing documents and on admission to a specialised educational institution. Third, in civil cases: annulment of marriage or recovery of maintenance. An examination is also needed in the investigation of sexual crimes when there is doubt about a person's registered sex.

The simultaneous presence of sex organs characteristic of both sexes is called hermaphroditism. True and false forms are distinguished. True hermaphroditism is very rare: both male and female gonads are present, that is, signs of spermatogenesis and oogenesis are found. The external features may resemble either male or female. In false hermaphroditism, by contrast, the gland belongs to one sex, while the external features resemble the other sex.

Let us compare the signs of false hermaphroditism. In a false male hermaphrodite the testis functions, but the external features resemble female ones: a small penis, cryptorchidism and enlargement of the mammary glands are observed. In a false female hermaphrodite the ovary functions, while the external features are male: clitoral hypertrophy and fusion of the labia majora. Remember, here the functioning gland corresponds to one sex, and the external appearance to the other.

Determination of sex is carried out in several stages. First, anamnestic data are collected: menstruation, nocturnal emissions, sexual desire. The records of the gynaecologist, urologist, andrologist and endocrinologist are taken into account. Then anthropometric measurements are made, and the external genitalia and secondary sexual characteristics are studied. Clinical, laboratory and functional examinations are also carried out. Genetic sex can be established by examining the chromosomes in blood leucocytes.

The concept of sexual maturity. Sexual maturity is the level of development that makes it possible to lead a sexual life without harm to health and further development. In women this is the ability to have sexual intercourse, to conceive, to carry a pregnancy, to give birth and to breastfeed an infant. In men it is the ability to have sexual intercourse and to fertilise. As a rule, persons under 14 years of age are considered sexually immature. The question arises in the interval from 14 years to the age of marriage.

The practical significance of determining maturity has changed over time. Formerly, such a need arose in cases of rape, lewd acts, loss of virginity in minors and early marriage. Now this significance has diminished, because in the Criminal Code liability is tied to a specific age. Articles 118 and 119 specify ages 18 and 14, while Articles 128 and 129 specify age 16.

Signs of maturity in girls are assessed by several indicators. General physical development, the external and internal genitalia, secondary characteristics, pelvic dimensions and menstruation are taken into account. The examination is carried out with the participation of an obstetrician-gynaecologist, with clinical and laboratory investigations. As a rule, by the age of 16-17 pelvic development allows a normal course of labour.

Let us consider the anthropometric indicators. At maturity, body length should be not less than 150 cm standing and 80 cm sitting, and chest circumference at rest not less than 78-80 cm. Pelvic dimensions: distance between the anterior superior iliac spines 26-27 cm, between the greater trochanters of the femurs 29 cm, external conjugate 17-18 cm. An important note: the indicators are relative. Sometimes a woman can safely bear a child even with smaller values.

What does the capacity for sexual intercourse and pregnancy depend on? The capacity for sexual intercourse is linked to adequate development of the external genitalia, in particular the vagina. Pregnancy is possible after ovulation, and ovulation depends on a properly formed menstrual cycle. Carrying a pregnancy depends on the development of the uterus and pelvis: at maturity the body of the uterus makes up 2/3 of its length and the cervix 1/3.

The need to establish virginity arises in cases of rape, sexual intercourse with a person under 16 years of age, or lewd acts against them. Virginity, that is, virginitas, is determined mainly by the anatomical integrity of the hymen. The hymen is a duplicature of the vaginal mucosa, located between the vaginal vestibule and the vagina.

t: Structure and types of the hymen
n: Structure and types of the hymen. In the hymen, the base, the free edge and the orifice are distinguished; there may be several orifices, or none at all. According to Nikitin and Serdyukov there are three types. The usual type includes annular, semilunar and other forms. The unusual type is rare. The very rare type includes, in particular, a hymen without an orifice. When describing the features of the hymen, a clock face is used for comparison.

Disruption of the hymen at first sexual intercourse is called defloration and leads to loss of virginity. But the integrity of the hymen may be disrupted in other circumstances too: by a finger, by various objects, or during surgery. In some cases defloration may not occur at intercourse. This is observed with elastic, distensible, low hymens with many natural notches.

Hymenal tears and their healing times. At intercourse a complete tear reaches the base of the hymen, while an incomplete tear does not reach the base. At first the tear bleeds and the tissue is swollen. By the end of the first week the inflammation subsides and granulation tissue appears. At the end of the second week and in the third week a scar forms. After three weeks it is not possible to determine the age of the injury.

t: Distinguishing a tear from a natural notch
n: It is important to distinguish a tear from a natural notch. Natural notches are found in different segments of the hymen. Tears, by contrast, most often occur in the lower segments, between 5 and 7 o'clock on the clock face. Most natural notches do not reach the base of the hymen, and the tissue at their edges does not differ from other areas. The edges of an old tear, however, are relatively thick and scarred.

t: Signs of intercourse; duties of physicians
n: Signs of sexual intercourse: semen found in the vagina, development of pregnancy and transmission of sexually transmitted diseases. Semen usually persists in the vagina for up to 3-5 days. Therefore, the sooner the sample is taken, the more reliable the result. Physicians must explain that, when there is suspicion, a forensic medical expert should be consulted as soon as possible.

Reproductive capacity in men is determined by the ability to have intercourse and to fertilise, and in women by the ability to have intercourse, to conceive and to give birth. The need for this examination arises in criminal cases involving bodily injury, child abduction and rape, as well as in civil cases on annulment of marriage and maintenance. The examination is carried out with the participation of the relevant clinical specialists, with laboratory and instrumental, and sometimes inpatient, investigation.

t: Impotence and fertilising capacity in men
n: Impotence in men may be due to diseases of the central nervous system, defects of the external genitalia, endocrine diseases or a neurotic reaction. Fertilising capacity is established by laboratory examination of the ejaculate. The finding of normally motile spermatozoa confirms this capacity. Azoospermia, necrospermia or asthenospermia, on the other hand, rule it out.

Impeding conditions in women are considered in three directions. Sexual intercourse is impeded by vaginal atresia, aplasia, scars, tumours, deformity of the pelvic bones and vaginismus. Conception is excluded by age, that is, before puberty or after the menopause, diseases of the genital organs, developmental defects, tumours and operations. Childbirth is impeded by a narrow pelvis and pelvic deformity.

t: Examination of pregnancy, delivery and abortion
n: Examination of pregnancy, delivery and abortion. The need for such an examination arises in crimes connected with infanticide, child abduction, criminal abortion, rape, lewd acts and bodily injury. The examinations are carried out with the participation of obstetrician-gynaecologists, with clinical-laboratory and instrumental investigations.

Signs of an ongoing pregnancy fall into three groups. Presumptive signs: absence of menstruation, enlargement of the mammary glands, nipple and areola, appearance of pigmentation, clearly evident from the 2nd month. Laboratory signs: chorionic gonadotropin is detected, and the size, shape and consistency of the uterus change. Positive signs: fetal heartbeat on auscultation, fetal parts and movements on palpation and ultrasound.

Signs of previous delivery change over time. In the first days the mammary glands are engorged, the areola is darker, and secretion is discharged; cytological examination of the breast secretion is important for determining the time elapsed. Initially the perineum is wide, the vaginal introitus is open and the labia are swollen; the external os of the cervix is open. Later, delivery is indicated by the slit-like shape of the external os of the cervix, myrtiform papillae and scars on the abdominal skin. At this stage it is possible only to record that delivery has taken place.

Abortion is the termination of pregnancy before 22 weeks. It may be spontaneous or induced. Spontaneous abortion occurs because of disease or poisoning. Induced abortion is divided into artificial, that is, medical, and criminal. Medical abortion is performed by obstetrician-gynaecologists up to 12 weeks at the woman's request, and later on medical and social indications.

Criminal abortion may be performed in a medical institution or outside it by untrained staff or by persons without medical education; this is defined by Article 114 of the Criminal Code. The examination studies the pregnancy and its termination, the method and the consequences. There are four kinds of method: mechanical, that is, medical instruments, objects or liquid under pressure; chemical, that is, medicines, acid, alkali, alcohol, soap; sometimes thermal, that is, hot water and hot baths; and, very rarely, the action of electric current.

The complications of criminal abortion can be severe. Life-threatening conditions: air embolism, traumatic shock, acute haemorrhage, perforation of the vagina or uterus. Poisoning by chemicals or drugs and infectious complications are also observed. They may be the direct cause of death.

A general concept of sexual crimes. In forensic medicine, rape, sodomy, lewd acts, and the spread of sexually transmitted diseases or HIV/AIDS are studied among sexual crimes. Rape, sodomy and acts in an unnatural manner are considered crimes against sexual freedom. The spread of a sexually transmitted disease and of HIV/AIDS, however, is a crime endangering life or health.

The definition of rape. Under Article 118 of the Criminal Code it is sexual intercourse against the will of the victim, using violence or threat, or taking advantage of her helpless state. In theory men too may be victims, but in practice it is observed mainly in relation to women. Remember: "rape" is a legal concept. The examination studies objective signs of intercourse or attempted intercourse, of violence and of helplessness.

Examination of the victim is carried out in a definite sequence. First the documents are reviewed: the order made before the direct examination, the record of the scene inspection and the medical records are studied. Then, by interview, the details of the incident are established and the gynaecological history is taken. After that the examination is carried out and samples are taken. Do not forget: intimidation leaves no characteristic objective signs on the victim.

Signs in rape are found in several areas. In violence there are bruises and abrasions on the skin, often on the inner surfaces of the thighs and in the genital area. In the genitalia, a hymenal tear is found, and in some cases haemorrhages and tears of the vaginal wall and perineum. An important note: injury to the vagina and perineum may also occur in women who lead an active sexual life.

Finding semen in the vagina and on the external genitalia, pubis, perineum and thighs is important evidence. After the incident, a vaginal smear and impression smears from external areas should be taken as soon as possible, because with time the probability of finding spermatozoa decreases. Helplessness may be related to several causes: mental illness, trauma, physical defect, young or old age, alcohol or narcotic intoxication, stupefying substances.

Satisfying a need in an unnatural manner by violence, threat or taking advantage of a helpless state is defined by Article 119 of the Criminal Code. At examination the oral cavity, the anus and the area around it, and the lower part of the rectum are examined; smears and impression smears are taken. In rape it is expedient to subject suspects to examination as well.

Sodomy is defined by Article 120 of the Criminal Code: it is the satisfaction of sexual need by a man with a man without the use of violence. Both the active and the passive participant are considered subjects of the offence. In the active participant, the other person's blood, hair, faecal particles and oily substances may be found on the penis and pubis. The passive participant has abrasions, haemorrhages and fissures; if regular, a funnel-shaped depression is observed.

Passive participant and differential diagnosis. With regular sexual intercourse the anus is funnel-shaped and depressed, the sphincter is weak, and the radial folds are smoothed. But constipation, diarrhoea, proctitis, paraproctitis, haemorrhoids, rectal prolapse and surgical scars may be misinterpreted; therefore a proctologist is consulted. If violence was used, only the active participant is liable under Article 119 of the Criminal Code; the passive participant is considered the victim.

t: Lewd acts (Article 129 of the Criminal Code)
n: Lewd acts are linked to Article 129 of the Criminal Code. Lewd acts are indecent, depraved acts against persons under sixteen years of age. Examples: touching a genital organ with a hand or penis, rubbing, exposing the genitalia, masturbation, showing pornographic images. In the Criminal Code this offence is placed in the group of crimes against the family, youth and morality.

Examination findings in lewd acts may vary. There may be redness, abrasion, bruising, haemorrhage in the vaginal mucosa, a superficial fissure, haemorrhage in the hymen or an incomplete tear. Traces of semen may be found on the external genitalia, in the thigh area or on clothing; a sample is taken. In some cases, however, lewd acts may leave no trace at all.

t: Sexually transmitted diseases and HIV/AIDS (Article 113 of the Criminal Code)
n: Article 113 of the Criminal Code establishes liability for knowingly infecting another person with a sexually transmitted disease or HIV/AIDS, or placing them at risk of infection. The examination is carried out with the participation of a dermatovenereologist and AIDS specialists; the presence of the disease and the source of infection are studied. The same article also provides for liability for HIV infection resulting from improper performance of official duties.

The classification of violence against children is given according to Simpson. In the United Kingdom, child abuse is classified as physical, emotional and sexual abuse and neglect; they may occur at the same time. Sexual abuse involves forcing or enticing a child into sexual activity: physical contact, non-contact acts and pornographic material.

t: Child sexual abuse: timing of examination (Simpson)
n: Child sexual abuse and the timing of examination according to Simpson. Presentation may be delayed from several days to years, which leads to the loss of forensic evidence. In pubertal and prepubertal girls, clear genital signs are more often seen when examined within 7 days of the last episode. Anal signs, by contrast, are more often seen in the acute stage, within the first 72 hours.

Principles of examining a child according to Simpson. The principles of examination are similar to those for adults, but issues of consent and documentation become more complicated. It is important to obtain a permanent record of genital or anal findings, that is, with a colposcope or camera. Genito-anal examination is stressful for the child; therefore it is done at the end of the general examination, and the risk of retraumatising the child is taken into account.

t: Interpreting the results of a child's examination (Simpson)
n: Interpreting the results of a child's examination. In most children who allege sexual abuse, no genito-anal changes are found. Interpreting findings is very difficult, so precise terminology is needed when describing changes. Some infections may be significant, but they must be assessed in context and in light of modern studies.
